source.title: CSULoRA: Closest Safe Update Low-Rank Adaptation
source.authors: Oleksandr Marchenko Breneur; Adelaide Danilov; A. Nourbakhsh; Salima Lamsiyah

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full paper, including its appendix.
record.tranche_reason: Tests safety behavior after adversarial fine-tuning of aligned chat models and reports harmful-prompt compliance rates, using a different training setup and models from the cited original work.
record.gate_note: The reported main experiment fine-tunes on a 95:5 mixture of benign and unsafe data, so it does not isolate the effect of benign-only training. The authors also state that preliminary benign-only fine-tuning effects were inconsistent across datasets and hyperparameters, without reporting model identities, conditions, or numerical outcomes. Table 1 reports ASR for several post-hoc correction methods; those results evaluate the methods, not whether safety is localized in a few parameters or deepened beyond initial tokens.
record.test_reason: This is a defence-method paper, but it reports standard-LoRA attack success rate before and after adversarial fine-tuning on two instruct models, which is a direct result on V1. The setting is new for this claim: small models, LoRA, 1,000 BeaverTails examples diluted 95:5 in benign data, and a regex refusal detector on AdvBench. Qi et al. used pure harmful sets and a GPT-4 judge. The measurement is close to the original's, but the dilution and the detector make this T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CSULoRA, a post-hoc closed-form correction of LoRA adapters, cuts AdvBench ASR to below base-model levels (1.73% and 1.35%) while keeping most IFEval utility gains and ARC capability, in their two-model adversarial fine-tuning setting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adversarial LoRA fine-tuning with a 95:5 benign/unsafe training mixture and AdvBench ASR evaluation; reports two instruction-tuned models and also evaluates post-hoc adapter corrections.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that benign-only fine-tuning effects varied across datasets and hyperparameters; no specific conditions or results are supplied. ASR and correction-method outcomes differ across the two tested models.
record.problems: Only two instruction-tuned models and one adversarial data mixture are tested. The ASR measure is a regex-based refusal detector and, as the authors note, does not evaluate actual response harmfulness as an LLM judge might. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The benign-only finding is summarized without numerical results or experimental details.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Table 1 results for SafeLoRA, SPLoRA, SaLoRA, AlignGuard, RESTA, and CSULoRA are not cataloged because they report post-hoc correction-method performance, not a test of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: The 'few to a few hundred examples' range: only 1,000 harmful examples in a 20k mixture are used, with no sweep over data size. Pure harmful-only fine-tuning, full fine-tuning, larger models, and judge-based harmfulness are also untested.
No benign-only results are reported. Neither ordinary nor selected benign data is quantified.
Not tested. The method uses base–aligned weight-displacement subspaces as a tool and reports only its own defence performance.
Not tested. Post-hoc adapter correction is not token-depth deepening.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's second V1 limits_scope label was removed. Using 1,000 rather than a few hundred examples is an untested part, not a qualifying result. V1 does not require near-total refusal removal, and a rise to about 50–60% ASR counts as observed. The defence-method rows from Table 1 are correctly left out. The V2 verdict rests only on an unquantified author remark, and researchers should weight it accordingly.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses 1,000 unsafe examples in a 20,000-example mixture, not a sweep over a few to a few hundred harmful examples. It does not establish that refusal is removed almost entirely.
The main experiment does not isolate benign-only fine-tuning. The preliminary benign-only finding has no stated models, datasets, hyperparameters, or numerical results.
The method uses weight-displacement subspaces to correct adapters, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The study does not investigate why safety might be shallow or measure first-token concentration.
The study evaluates post-hoc adapter correction, not training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens or the robustness of such training.

rows.note: Control/reference result for the fine-tuned model.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: LoRA fine-tuning on 20,000 examples: 19,000 benign constrained-instruction samples and 1,000 unsafe samples (95:5 mixture).
rows.note: Unsafe compliance increased substantially after fine-tuning, though the study does not test the claimed few-to-few-hundred-example range.
rows.check: The training data are 1,000 harmful examples mixed into 19,000 benign ones, not a pure harmful set. ASR is the share of responses with no regex-detected refusal, not judged harmfulness.

relationships.condition: Standard LoRA (r=16, attention projections, 3 epochs) on a 95:5 benign/BeaverTails-unsafe mixture; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4B-it; AdvBench with regex refusal ASR
relationships.reason: ASR rises from 2.69% to 60.58% for Llama (R1, R2) and from 2.50% to 48.85% for Gemma (R3, R4), even with harmful data at only 5%.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success rose from 2.69% to 60.58% for Llama-3.2-3B and from 2.50% to 48.85% for Gemma-3-4B, with harmful data only 5% of the mix.
